lessons.title: ESOPs, RSUs, SARs and Sweat Equity: The Employee Equity Family

children.text: Read enough Indian offer letters and you will meet four different animals wearing the same coat. One says "5,000 ESOPs". Another says "3,000 RSUs vesting over four years". A third offers "stock appreciation rights". A founder tells an early employee she will get "sweat equity". Most people nod, sign, and only find out the difference years later, usually when money is at stake.
They are genuinely different instruments, with different costs, different risks and different tax treatment. This lesson sorts them out.

body.text: Two questions separate every employee equity instrument: do I have to pay anything to get the shares, and do I end up with shares or with cash?

children.text: The Family Tree
An
ESOP
is the most common instrument in Indian startups, but it is one of several. Here is the whole family in one table.

markDefs.definition: Employee Stock Option: the right, not the obligation, to buy a fixed number of shares at a pre-decided exercise price after vesting.

body.text: In everyday Indian usage, people say "ESOPs" for all of these. Your offer letter is not a definition. Always ask for the scheme document and check which instrument you are actually being granted.

children.text: ESOP vs RSU: The Comparison That Matters Most
An ESOP is a right to buy. An
RSU
is a promise to give. With an RSU there is no exercise price to pay, or at most the
par value
of the share. Infosys, for instance, grants RSUs with an exercise price equal to the par value of the share, while its stock options carry the market price on the grant date.

markDefs.definition: Restricted Stock Unit: a promise to give the employee actual shares once conditions are met, with nothing to pay or only the par value of the share.
The nominal value of a share stated in the company’s capital structure, often ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 or ₹10. It is unrelated to market price.

children.text: That difference has one huge consequence. An RSU is worth something as long as the share is worth something. An ESOP is worth nothing unless the share value climbs above the exercise price.
Worked example.

Two employees join the same listed company at a share price of ₹100. Arjun gets 1,000 ESOPs at an exercise price of ₹100. Priya gets 250 RSUs with a par value of ₹1. Fewer units for Priya, because RSUs cost the company more per unit. Here is what each grant is worth at different share prices once vested.

body.title: Pre-tax value of the two grants at different share prices

children.text: Notice the shape. If the share falls to ₹80, Arjun's options are worthless and Priya still holds ₹19,750. But if the share triples to ₹400, Arjun is at ₹3,00,000 against Priya's ₹99,750.
RSUs are the safer instrument. ESOPs are the leveraged one.

columns.label: ESOPs
points: You pay an exercise price to convert options into shares
Worth zero if the share value stays below the exercise price
Higher upside per unit if the company does well
Needs cash from you at the moment of exercise
Standard at Indian startups, from seed stage onwards

columns.label: RSUs
points: Nothing to pay, or only the par value of the share
Retains value as long as the share has value
Usually granted in smaller numbers for the same package value
Shares simply arrive in your account on vesting
Common at listed firms and Indian employees of global companies

body.title: Value the RSU Grant
body.prompt: Priya's 250 RSUs vest when the share price is ₹600. She pays only the par value of ₹1 per share. What is her pre-tax gain?
body.explanation: Gain per unit = ₹600 minus ₹1 = ₹599. Total = ₹599 × 250 = ₹1,49,750. An ESOP holder at a ₹100 exercise price would have gained ₹500 per option instead, but would have had to pay ₹1,00,000 to exercise.

children.text: SARs: The Gain Without the Cheque
A
Stock Appreciation Right
pays you the increase in share value above a base price, and you never pay an exercise price. If the company settles in cash, you never even become a shareholder.

markDefs.definition: Stock Appreciation Right: a right to receive the increase in share value above a base price, settled in cash or in shares, without the employee paying an exercise price.

body.latex: \text{SAR payout} = (\text{Share value on exercise} - \text{Base price}) \times \text{Number of SARs}
body.caption: Settled either as cash, or as shares of equivalent value.

children.text: Example: Neha holds 2,000 SARs with a base price of ₹150. The share is now valued at ₹260. Her payout is ₹2,20,000. If the company settles in cash, that amount reaches her bank account. If it settles in shares, she receives roughly 846 shares worth about the same, without paying anything.

body.text: SEBI’s SBEB and Sweat Equity Regulations, 2021 cover equity-settled SARs for listed companies. Cash-settled SARs fall outside them because no shares are issued. If your grant is cash settled, you are holding a bonus formula, not ownership. No shareholder rights, no capital gains treatment.

children.text: ESPS and Sweat Equity: Shares Without the Waiting
Employee Stock Purchase Scheme
Under an
ESPS

, the company offers you shares directly, usually at a discount. Suppose your employer offers 400 shares at a 25% discount to a market price of ₹500. You pay ₹375 per share, so ₹1,50,000 in total, and the discount is worth ₹50,000. You own the shares immediately, subject to any lock-in the scheme sets.

markDefs.definition: Employee Stock Purchase Scheme: a scheme under which employees are offered the company’s shares directly, usually at a discount to market price.

children.text: Sweat equity
Sweat equity shares

are not options at all. They are real shares issued now, at a discount or for a non-cash contribution such as intellectual property, technical know-how or significant value addition. They are governed by Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013, need a special resolution, and come with hard limits.

markDefs.definition: Sweat equity shares: shares a company issues to employees or directors at a discount or for non-cash consideration such as know-how or intellectual property, under Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013.

stats.label: In any one year
stats.context: Of existing paid-up equity capital, or shares worth ₹5 crore, whichever is higher

stats.label: Overall ceiling
stats.context: Of paid-up capital at any time, for most companies

stats.label: DPIIT-recognised startups
stats.context: Higher ceiling, available up to 10 years from incorporation

body.text: Sweat equity is why a technical co-founder who joins after incorporation can be given real shares for building the product, rather than options she would have to buy later.

children.text: Phantom Stock: Ownership Without Ownership
Phantom stock

mimics the payoff of shares while issuing none. The employee gets a cash amount linked to the share value at a future date. Companies like it because there is no dilution and no cap table entry. Employees should read it for what it is: a deferred cash bonus that depends on the company having cash to pay when the time comes.

markDefs.definition: Phantom stock: a cash bonus whose size tracks the company’s share value. No shares are ever issued and the employee never becomes a shareholder.

body.title: Identify the Instrument
body.question: An employee is told: "You will receive the increase in our share value above ₹200 per unit, paid to you in cash after three years. You pay nothing, and you will not appear on our shareholder register." What is being offered?
options: A cash-settled SAR or phantom stock
body.explanation: Nothing to pay, cash settlement, and no entry on the shareholder register. That rules out ESOPs and RSUs, which both end in shares, and sweat equity, which issues shares immediately. This is a cash-settled appreciation right, economically the same as phantom stock.

body.title: The Defining Difference
body.textWithBlank: The single biggest difference between an ESOP and an RSU is that only the ESOP holder must pay an ___ price to receive the shares.
body.explanation: An RSU holder pays nothing, or at most the par value of the share. That is why RSUs keep some value even when the share price falls, while ESOPs can expire worthless.

body.title: Why do Indian startups give ESOPs rather than RSUs?

children.text: Three practical reasons. First, an unlisted company has no daily market price, so an RSU that hands over shares on vesting creates an immediate tax event on a valuation nobody can sell against. Second, ESOPs let a startup grant a large number of units cheaply, because each one only carries value above the exercise price, which suits a company betting on a big increase in value. Third, the exercise step gives employees a choice: if the company has not done well, they can walk away without spending anything.

RSUs are far more common where shares are liquid, which is why Indian employees of Google, Microsoft, Amazon and other global firms usually hold RSUs of the overseas parent, and large listed Indian firms use them for senior talent.

body.title: Questions to Ask Before You Accept Any Equity Grant
steps: Which instrument is this exactly: ESOP, RSU, SAR, ESPS, sweat equity or phantom stock?
Do I pay anything, and if so how much per share?
Do I end up holding shares, or only receiving cash?
Which company’s shares are these: the Indian entity or an overseas parent?
Over what period does it vest, and what happens if I leave?
When and how can I actually convert this into money?
When is tax triggered, and who deducts it?

body.title: Designing the Right Mix
body.scenario: Shalini heads HR at a 200-person listed manufacturing company in Chennai. The board wants to reward three groups: 12 senior leaders whom competitors keep poaching, 40 plant supervisors with modest salaries who would struggle to fund any exercise price, and the whole employee base, as a gesture of shared ownership.
body.prompt: Which instrument suits each group, and why?
body.modelAnswer: For the 12 senior leaders, ESOPs work well: they can fund the exercise price, they have the most influence over company performance, and the leverage of an exercise price sharpens the retention effect. For the 40 plant supervisors, an instrument with nothing to pay is fairer, so RSUs or equity-settled SARs avoid asking people on modest salaries to find cash to exercise. For the full employee base, an ESPS lets everyone buy shares at a discount in a single, simple, well-understood offer. Since the company is listed, all three routes must follow the SEBI SBEB and Sweat Equity Regulations, 2021, with shareholder approval by special resolution.

children.text: One Line on Tax, Before Chapter 4

Tax follows the instrument, not the label. Broadly, when shares are received free or cheap, the discount is taxed as a salary perquisite under Section 17(1)(d) read with Section 17(5)(h) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 [Section 17(2)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961], and any later increase in value is taxed as capital gains when you sell. A cash-settled SAR or phantom payout is simply salary income when paid. Chapter 4 works through each case with numbers.

body.label: Check any listed company’s ESOP disclosures on screener.in
body.description: Open a company, then read its annual report notes. Listed companies must disclose options granted, exercised and outstanding, plus the exercise price range.

cards.definition: Right to buy shares at an exercise price after vesting. Can expire worthless.
Shares delivered on vesting for nothing, or only par value. Keeps value while the share does.
Pays only the appreciation above a base price, in cash or shares. Nothing to pay.
Buy company shares directly, usually at a discount to market price.
Real shares issued now for know-how, IP or value addition, under Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013.
Cash bonus that tracks the share price. No shares, no shareholder rights.

points: Ask two questions of any grant: do I pay anything, and do I receive shares or cash?
ESOPs need an exercise price and can expire worthless. RSUs cost nothing or only par value and retain value while the share does.
SARs pay only the appreciation above a base price. Cash-settled SARs and phantom stock give you no ownership at all.

ESPS lets employees buy shares directly at a discount. Sweat equity issues real shares for know-how or IP under Section 54, capped at 25% of paid-up capital, or 50% for DPIIT-recognised startups within 10 years of incorporation.
Indian startups favour ESOPs, while RSUs dominate at listed firms and at Indian arms of global companies.
The word "ESOP" is used loosely in India. Read the scheme document, not the offer letter headline.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Scheme terms and tax outcomes vary with the instrument, the employer and your own situation. Read your scheme document and consult a qualified professional.
